$comment: Every number this page draws, tied to the committed blob it came from.
The page's thesis is 'every number is traceable to the repository it came
from'. Until this file existed that was a slogan: the plates and the prose
were checked against EACH OTHER (gate.mjs check 9) and against nothing else,
so two authored strings could agree perfectly and both be false. Three rounds
of audits found exactly that.
A row is a derivation, not a citation. `extractor` is a shell command run
against $BLOB — the file fetched from raw.githubusercontent.com at `ref`,
which is a COMMIT SHA, never a branch name. Its stdout must equal `value`
exactly. Nobody has to trust the number; they run the command.
`drawn_on` is where the value appears on this page. build/claims.mjs checks
both directions: every row must re-derive, AND every number a plate draws
must have a row here or an entry in `exempt`. A claims file that only
verified the numbers it happened to list would be the same gate-that-cannot-
fail this project has already shipped twice.

applied-web.note: The in-browser ONNX build is NOT on main. The commit is pushed and public, so it pins and re-derives like any other — but the page must say which branch it is reading, and does.

automl.note: Public since 2026-07-30. Every AutoML figure on this page was ATTESTED before that and is now DERIVED, which is the whole point of the distinction. Written with Shree Chaturvedi; the repository has disjoint histories, so main is the only branch worth pinning.

claims.note: Parsed, not grepped. A second method — counting r-string lines inside the PATTERNS block — also gives 201.

claims.extractor: grep -cE '^ALTER TABLE .* FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY' "$BLOB"
claims.note: Anchored to ^ALTER TABLE on purpose. A bare `grep -c 'FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY'` returns 8, because the file's own header comment explains what FORCE does — the same prose-counting mistake as the row above, in a file where it would have inflated the claim. user_profiles is deliberately excluded from RLS (0002_enable_rls.sql:21-22), so 'every tenant table' is seven, and the README now says seven.

The canonical Adler-32 vector for the input "Wikipedia", asserted for both the scalar and the vectorised path (Adler32Test.java:36-37). It is now drawn as one string per row rather than eight <text> elements, so it appears whole in the plate and needs no per-glyph exemptions. The stronger claim on the plate — bit-identical to java.util.zip — is the separate matchesJdkAcrossSizes test, which compares both paths across 26 input sizes.

Counted from the guard in the QUERY, not from a comment about it. The previous row here counted the word IDOR in docstrings and returned 7; four different methods return 7, 8, 9 and 15, so the count of vulnerabilities is an audit finding and belongs in prose. How many services now scope by owner is a property of the code.

The page's strongest single piece of evidence, and it was uncited. The binary getglyph.vercel.app serves is byte-identical to this blob, so 'it came off a branch carrying real wasm_simd128 intrinsics' stops being testimony: curl the URL, hash it, compare.
0.979 with no uncertainty beside it was the page's one remaining asymmetry: jetpack's numbers all carry an interval and Applied's did not. The honest statement of a 96-row result is the error count.
The set is balanced 12 per class, which is why macro-F1 and weighted-F1 are identical to the last digit. Unstated until now, and it is the reason the two numbers agree.
User, Quest, QuestProgress, Reward, Redemption, Meetup, ResumePrompt, Session, ContentGeneration, RitualLog. Deliberately apps/api and not legacy/backend, whose older schema has 6.
Every file carrying an @Controller decorator in apps/api/src. Route-method decorators, not handler methods, so a method serving two verbs counts twice — which is what an endpoint count should mean.
auth, health, meetups, quests, rewards, users.
Counted two ways and they agree: the seven files sum 4+8+3+6+14+6+3, and a single grep across all seven returns 44.

LLM_TOOL_DEFINITIONS in tools/index.ts is data + cell + package only. This is the number that makes the routing claim concrete: 44 tools exist, and the general set the model carries everywhere is 15 of them.

Seven exported phase sets: onboarding, preprocessing, feature proposal, feature continue, feature engineering, feature lifecycle, training lifecycle. LLM_ALL_TOOLS is excluded because it is the union, not a phase.

Two methods agree: 29 CREATE TABLE statements, and 29 distinct table names after lowercasing and deduplicating. Eleven of the 24 migrations create tables (7+3+3+6+1+1+1+1+1+4+1); the other thirteen alter, backfill or index, and listing them would only pad the fetch.
The container is --read-only with --network none, so these five tmpfs mounts are the entire writable surface the generated Python gets. Drawing the count is drawing the size of the blast radius.

$unpinnable_note: This list held exactly one row — AutoML's '2 approval gates' — filed under
the reason 'the repo is private'. That diagnosis was wrong, and the way it
was wrong matters more than the number.
The count was not merely unverifiable. It was FALSE: the reproducible count
of human-gate stages is four (preprocessing await_approval, feature
engineering await_review, training propose_model and await_review). By
filing it as 'private, therefore unpinnable' this file certified a wrong
number as an acceptable one, and printed a friendly note where it should
have failed. A category that excuses a claim from being checked will,
sooner or later, be where a false claim goes to live.
So there is no such category any more. Plate VI no longer draws a count at
all; it draws the mechanism and says on its face that this is the one
section a reader cannot check. Anything drawn must derive or be exempt.

external.why: Vercel's Hobby-tier cap of 12 Vercel Functions per deployment is a platform fact (the docs moved: /docs/limits now says 'framework-dependent', and the 12 lives at the runtimes page cited above), not a measurement of this repository. The previous extractor grepped `caps deployments at 12` out of api/index.ts — the author's own comment — so the page was citing itself and calling it derivation. What the repo genuinely proves is the consequence: one function serving 36 routes, which cadence.handlers derives.

$attested_note: Facts about the AUTHOR rather than measurements of a repository.
Everything in `claims` is re-derived in CI from a pinned commit, and that is
the page's whole argument. A year of internship work is not in any repository
a reader can clone: the Oracle logs, the Tableau inventory and the compliance
dashboard belong to Miami University. Nor is a competition result.
Those facts are worth putting on the page, and pretending they carry the same
warrant as `422 MB/s` would be exactly the move this document exists to
refuse. So they live here, they are labelled ATTESTED on the plate that draws
them, and claims.mjs prints them separately from the derived set. The reader
is told which numbers they can check and which they are taking on trust.
